dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: Contoso is selecting a pricing tier for a new App Service plan that will host an internal line-of-business web app. The app must run on virtual machine instances that are dedicated to Contoso and not shared with other Azure customers. Contoso wants the lowest-cost tier that meets this requirement. Which pricing tier should you select?
spiegazione: Basic (B1) is correct. Microsoft Learn groups App Service pricing tiers into three compute categories: shared compute (Free, Shared), dedicated compute (Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3, PremiumV4) and isolated (IsolatedV2). Basic is the lowest tier in the dedicated compute category, where apps run on dedicated Azure VMs and only apps in the same App Service plan share those compute resources. Free (F1) is wrong because the Free tier is shared compute: the app runs on the same VM as other App Service apps, including apps belonging to other customers. Shared (D1) is wrong for the same reason - Shared is the second shared-compute base tier and also places the app on a VM shared with other customers; it only adds a per-app CPU quota and custom domain support. Standard (S1) is wrong not because it fails the requirement (Standard is dedicated compute) but because it is a higher, more expensive tier than Basic, so it is not the lowest-cost tier that satisfies the dedicated-VM requirement.
tags: app service, app service plan, pricing tier, dedicated compute, shared compute, basic tier

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: An App Service plan named ASP1 uses the Standard (S1) pricing tier. What is the maximum number of instances that ASP1 can be scaled out to?
spiegazione: 10 is correct. The documented App Service scale-out limits are 3 dedicated instances for Basic, 10 dedicated instances for Standard, 20 for Premium v1, 30 for Premium v2/v3/v4, and 100 for Isolated. Free and Shared cannot scale out at all (1 shared instance). 3 is wrong because that is the Basic tier scale-out maximum, not Standard. 20 is wrong because that is the Premium (v1) maximum; it is also the number of deployment slots per app in the Premium and Isolated tiers, which is a common source of confusion. 30 is wrong because that is the scale-out maximum for the Premium v2, v3 and v4 tiers, and is also the ceiling for the Maximum burst setting when automatic scaling is enabled on a Premium v2-v4 plan.
tags: app service, app service plan, scale out, instance limits, standard tier, service limits

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: Four web apps are hosted in a single App Service plan named ASP1 that uses the Premium v3 (P1v3) pricing tier. Which statements about this configuration are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: All four apps run on the same VM instances that are configured in ASP1.
opzione_b: Scaling out ASP1 to additional instances affects all four apps.
opzione_c: Each of the four apps can be assigned its own pricing tier within ASP1.
opzione_d: Deployment slots created for the apps run on the same VM instances as ASP1.
opzione_e: The storage limit of the Premium v3 tier applies separately to each of the four apps.
spiegazione: Options a, b and d are correct. Microsoft Learn states that when an app runs, it runs on all the VM instances configured in the App Service plan; if multiple apps are in the same plan, they all share the same VM instances; and if an app has multiple deployment slots, all deployment slots also run on those same VM instances (Learn further notes that an active slot is classified as an active app because it competes for resources in the same plan). All apps in a plan scale together because they share the same underlying compute resources, so scaling the plan - manually or through autoscale - affects every app in it. Option c is wrong because the pricing tier is a property of the App Service plan, not of the individual app; to give an app a different tier you must move it to a separate App Service plan. Option e is wrong because the documented storage limit (250 GB for Premium) is the total content size across all apps in the same App Service plan, not a per-app allowance.
tags: app service, app service plan, shared compute resources, deployment slots, storage limit, premium v3

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: A web app named App1 runs in an App Service plan that uses the Basic (B2) pricing tier. The operations team must configure rules that automatically add instances when the average CPU percentage exceeds a threshold and remove instances when CPU drops. You need to make the smallest change that enables this capability. What should you do?
opzione_a: Enable automatic scaling on the existing Basic plan and set Maximum burst to 10.
opzione_b: Scale out the existing Basic plan manually to 3 instances.
opzione_c: Scale up the App Service plan to the Standard tier.
opzione_d: Scale up the App Service plan to the Premium v3 tier.
spiegazione: Scaling up to the Standard tier is correct. The App Service scale-out options table on Microsoft Learn shows that manual scaling is available on Basic and up, rule-based autoscale is available on Standard and up, and automatic scaling is available on Premium v2 through v4. Metric-based scale rules therefore require at minimum the Standard tier, and Standard is the smallest change from Basic. Option a is wrong on two counts: automatic scaling is not available on Basic plans, and automatic scaling is traffic-based rather than rule-based - it explicitly does not use CPU or memory rules. Option b is wrong because manual scaling only fixes a static instance count; it provides no rules and no automatic reaction to CPU. Option d is wrong because although Premium v3 does support autoscale, it is a larger and more expensive change than necessary; the requirement is the smallest change.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale rules, standard tier, scale up, automatic scaling

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: A prototype web app currently runs in an App Service plan that uses the Free (F1) tier and is reachable only at proto.azurewebsites.net. Marketing now requires the app to respond at www.contoso.com. You must meet the requirement at the lowest possible cost. What should you do first?
opzione_a: Add the custom domain to the app while leaving the plan in the Free (F1) tier.
opzione_b: Scale up the App Service plan to the Shared (D1) tier.
opzione_c: Scale up the App Service plan to the Basic (B1) tier.
opzione_d: Scale up the App Service plan to the Standard (S1) tier.
spiegazione: Scaling up to the Shared (D1) tier is correct. The App Service limits table shows that the Free tier supports 0 custom domains and is restricted to the azurewebsites.net subdomain, while the Shared tier and every higher tier support up to 500 custom domains. The App Service plan overview reinforces this by describing exactly this progression: start on Free, and when you add your custom DNS name to the web app, scale the plan up to the Shared tier. Option a is wrong because a custom DNS name cannot be mapped to an app in the Free tier at all. Options c and d are wrong not because they fail technically - Basic and Standard both support 500 custom domains - but because they are higher-priced tiers than Shared, and the requirement is the lowest possible cost. Note that a TLS/SSL binding for that custom domain would require Basic or higher, but the stated requirement here is only the custom domain mapping.
tags: app service, app service plan, custom domain, free tier, shared tier, scale up

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: App1 is a Windows web app that runs in an App Service plan named ASP1. ASP1 uses the Basic (B1) tier, is deployed to the East US region, and belongs to a resource group named RG1. App1 has no virtual network integration configured. You must move App1 to a different App Service plan. Which plan is a valid target for App1?
opzione_a: ASP2: Windows, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG1
opzione_b: ASP3: Windows, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG2
opzione_c: ASP4: Windows, Standard (S1), West US, resource group RG1
opzione_d: ASP5: Linux, Standard (S1), East US, resource group RG1
spiegazione: ASP2 is correct. Microsoft Learn states that you can move an app to another App Service plan only as long as the source plan and the target plan are in the same resource group, the same geographical region, and are of the same OS type. ASP2 matches ASP1 on all three: RG1, East US, and Windows. The pricing tier difference (B1 to S1) is irrelevant - the tiers do not have to match. ASP3 is wrong because it is in a different resource group (RG2). This also breaks the underlying webspace requirement: plans are deployed into a webspace determined by the resource group, region and OS combination, and an app can only move between plans in the same webspace. ASP4 is wrong because it is in a different region (West US); the region of a plan cannot be changed, and running the app elsewhere would require app cloning instead. ASP5 is wrong because it is a Linux plan; Learn explicitly says any change in type, such as Windows to Linux, is not supported.
tags: app service, app service plan, move app, webspace, resource group, operating system

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: You plan to enable automatic scaling (not rule-based autoscale) for a set of web apps in Azure App Service. Which statements about automatic scaling are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Automatic scaling is available only on Premium v2, Premium v3, and Premium v4 plans.
opzione_b: Automatic scaling requires you to define metric rules based on CPU and memory thresholds.
opzione_c: For a Premium v3 plan, the Maximum burst value can be set to as many as 30 instances.
opzione_d: The Always ready instances setting specifies the minimum number of instances for a web app.
opzione_e: Automatic scaling supports scaling deployment slot traffic.
spiegazione: Options a, c and d are correct. The scale-out options table on Microsoft Learn lists the available tiers for automatic scaling as Premium v2 - v4 (compared with Basic and up for manual scaling and Standard and up for autoscale). Learn states that for Premium v2, v3 and v4 plans you can specify a Maximum burst of up to 30 instances, and that the maximum burst number must be equal to or greater than the number of workers specified for the plan. The app-level Always ready instances setting specifies the minimum number of instances; if load exceeds that minimum, additional instances are added up to the plan's Maximum burst value. Option b is wrong because that describes autoscale, not automatic scaling: automatic scaling is traffic-based and has no rule-based or schedule-based scaling - Learn advises using autoscale instead if you need CPU-, memory- or time-based scaling. Option e is wrong because Learn explicitly notes that automatic scaling is not supported for deployment slot traffic.
tags: app service, automatic scaling, maximum burst, always ready instances, prewarmed instances, premium v3

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda:
An App Service plan named ASP1 uses the Free (F1) pricing tier, is deployed to the East US region, and hosts a single Windows web app named App1. App1 has started to receive unpredictable bursts of traffic and the team also wants to secure a custom domain with a certificate. Evaluate each of the following proposed statements and determine whether each one is achievable in the current configuration.

1. Scaling out ASP1 to three instances will improve App1's availability during traffic bursts.
2. Scaling up ASP1 to the Basic (B1) tier will allow you to configure a TLS/SSL binding for a custom domain on App1.
3. Configuring metric-based autoscale rules on ASP1 will automatically add instances when average CPU exceeds 70 percent.
opzione_a: Scaling out ASP1 to three instances will improve App1's availability during traffic bursts.
opzione_b: Scaling up ASP1 to the Basic (B1) tier will allow you to configure a TLS/SSL binding for a custom domain on App1.
opzione_c: Configuring metric-based autoscale rules on ASP1 will automatically add instances when average CPU exceeds 70 percent.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No. In the Free and Shared tiers an app receives CPU minutes on a shared VM instance and cannot scale out; the documented scale-out limit for both Free and Shared is 1 shared instance. Scaling out is only possible from the Basic tier upward (3 for Basic, 10 for Standard, 30 for Premium v2-v4, 100 for Isolated). Statement 2 is Yes. Microsoft Learn describes exactly this progression: you add a custom DNS name by scaling up to Shared, and when you want to create a TLS binding you scale up to the Basic tier. Basic is therefore sufficient for a TLS/SSL binding on a custom domain. Statement 3 is No. Rule-based autoscale requires the Standard tier or higher, as shown in the App Service scale-out options table (manual = Basic and up, autoscale = Standard and up, automatic scaling = Premium v2-v4). A Free-tier plan cannot have autoscale rules at all, so no CPU rule would ever add instances.
tags: app service, free tier, scale out, tls binding, autoscale, pricing tier features

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: Fabrikam hosts a web app in an App Service plan that currently uses the Basic (B2) pricing tier. The operations team has two new requirements: the plan must support metric-based autoscale rules, and the app must support five deployment slots for staged releases. You will scale the plan up to the lowest pricing tier that satisfies both requirements. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Lowest pricing tier that satisfies both requirements: [Basic (B2) | Standard (S2) | Premium v3 (P1v3)]
opzione_b: Maximum number of instances that tier can scale out to: [3 | 10 | 30]
opzione_c: Maximum number of deployment slots per app that tier supports: [0 | 5 | 20]
spiegazione: Standard (S2) is the lowest tier that satisfies both requirements. Rule-based autoscale is available on Standard and up, and deployment slots require the Standard, Premium or Isolated tier - the Basic tier supports no deployment slots and no autoscale rules. Premium v3 would satisfy both requirements as well, but it is not the lowest such tier. The Standard tier scale-out maximum is 10 dedicated instances (Basic is 3, Premium v2-v4 is 30, Isolated is 100). The Standard tier supports 5 deployment slots per app (Free, Shared and Basic support none; Premium v1-v4 and Isolated support 20). Note that because Standard supports exactly 5 slots, this plan is at the documented limit - Learn warns that an app with more than five slots cannot be scaled down to the Standard tier.
tags: app service, app service plan, standard tier, deployment slots, autoscale, scale out limits

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: An autoscale setting is applied to an App Service plan that uses the Premium v3 tier. The default profile has instance limits of minimum 2, maximum 10, and default 3. The profile contains two scale-out rules: Rule1 increases the instance count by 2 when the average CPU percentage is greater than 70, and Rule2 increases the instance count by 5 when the average memory percentage is greater than 80. The plan is currently running 3 instances when both Rule1 and Rule2 are triggered during the same autoscale evaluation. How many instances will the plan run after the scale action completes?
spiegazione: 8 is correct. Microsoft Learn documents that after autoscale selects a profile, it evaluates all scale-out rules in that profile. If more than one scale-out rule is triggered, autoscale calculates the new capacity determined by the scaleAction of each rule and scales to the highest specified capacity to ensure service availability. Rule1 yields 3 + 2 = 5 instances and Rule2 yields 3 + 5 = 8 instances; autoscale takes the higher value, 8, which is within the maximum of 10. Option a (3) is wrong because it assumes the rules cancel each other out or that autoscale requires all scale-out rules to agree; that AND behaviour applies to scale-in rules, where autoscale only scales in if all scale-in rules are triggered. Option b (5) is wrong because it applies only Rule1, but autoscale does not pick the first or the smallest scale-out result. Option d (10) is wrong because autoscale does not jump to the maximum instance limit when rules trigger - the maximum is a ceiling that prevents scaling beyond 10, not a target.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale out rules, autoscale evaluation, azure monitor, instance limits

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda: The autoscale setting for an App Service plan contains a single default profile with two scale-in rules. Rule3 decreases the instance count by 1 when the average CPU percentage is less than 25. Rule4 decreases the instance count by 1 when the HTTP queue length is less than 10. The plan is running 6 instances with a minimum instance limit of 2. During an autoscale evaluation, no scale-out rules are triggered, average CPU is 15 percent, and the HTTP queue length is 40. What happens?
opzione_a: Autoscale scales in by 1 instance to 5 instances because Rule3 is triggered.
opzione_b: No scale-in action occurs, because autoscale only scales in when every scale-in rule in the profile is triggered.
opzione_c: Autoscale scales in to the minimum of 2 instances because the profile's scale-in rules take precedence over the current capacity.
opzione_d: Autoscale scales in by 2 instances to 4 instances, applying both scale-in rules cumulatively.
spiegazione: Option b is correct. Microsoft Learn states that if no scale-out rules are triggered, autoscale evaluates the scale-in rules, and that autoscale only scales in if all the scale-in rules are triggered. Rule3 is satisfied (CPU 15 is less than 25) but Rule4 is not (HTTP queue length is 40, which is not less than 10), so the AND condition is not met and no scale-in occurs. Option a is wrong because it applies the OR behaviour that governs scale-out rules to scale-in rules; scale-out uses OR and takes the highest resulting capacity, while scale-in uses AND. Option c is wrong because the minimum instance limit is a floor that prevents autoscale from scaling below 2 instances - it is never a scale-in target, and no scale-in is triggered here anyway. Option d is wrong on two counts: the scale-in condition is not met, and even when multiple scale-in rules do trigger, autoscale does not add their actions together; it scales in by as little as possible, choosing the result that yields the highest capacity, to protect service availability.
tags: app service, autoscale, scale in rules, autoscale evaluation, azure monitor, flapping

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda:
An autoscale setting named AS1 targets an App Service plan named ASP1 that uses the Premium v3 tier. AS1 contains only a default profile with the following configuration:
- Instance limits: minimum = 2, maximum = 10, default = 5
- Scale-out rule: metric Percentage CPU, time aggregation Average, duration 10 minutes, operator GreaterThan, threshold 75, action Increase count by 2, cool down 5 minutes
- Scale-in rule: metric Percentage CPU, time aggregation Average, duration 10 minutes, operator LessThan, threshold 25, action Decrease count by 1, cool down 5 minutes
ASP1 is currently running 2 instances. Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: When the scale-out rule is triggered for the first time, the instance count becomes: [3 | 4 | 10]
opzione_b: If autoscale cannot read the Percentage CPU metric, autoscale: [takes no action | scales out to 5 instances | scales in to 2 instances]
opzione_c: If average CPU drops to 10 percent and stays there, the instance count becomes: [0 | 1 | 2]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: 4. The scale-out rule's scaleAction is Increase count by 2, so the new capacity is 2 + 2 = 4, which is within the maximum of 10. It is not 3 (that would be an increase of 1) and it is not 10 (autoscale does not jump to the maximum instance limit; the maximum is only a ceiling). Dropdown 2: scales out to 5 instances. Microsoft Learn describes the capacity.default element as follows: if there's a problem reading the resource metric and the current capacity is below the default, autoscale scales out to the default to ensure the availability of the resource. Current capacity is 2, which is below the default of 5, so autoscale scales out to 5. (If the current capacity were already higher than the default, autoscale would not scale in.) Dropdown 3: 2. The scale-in rule is triggered because average CPU of 10 is less than the threshold of 25, and the action would decrease the count by 1 to 1 instance. However, capacity.minimum ensures that autoscale doesn't scale the resource below the configured minimum, which is 2. The count therefore remains at 2. It is never 0, because a minimum of 2 is enforced.
tags: app service, autoscale, default capacity, instance limits, scale in, azure monitor, autoscale profile

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
domanda:
Case study: Litware, Inc. runs a public e-commerce site in an App Service plan named ASP-Prod that uses the Premium v3 (P1v3) pricing tier in the West Europe region. ASP-Prod hosts three web apps. During weekday business hours the traffic is steady and two instances are sufficient. However, every Friday from 18:00 to 23:00 Litware runs a flash-sale event that drives a large but entirely predictable traffic spike, and the apps must already have extra capacity in place when the event starts rather than adding instances only after the load arrives. Outside business hours, traffic is minimal and Litware wants to minimize cost. The operations team wants a single, native configuration on ASP-Prod and does not want to rely on reactive metric thresholds alone.

What should you configure?
opzione_a: An autoscale setting with a single default profile that contains a Percentage CPU scale-out rule, with instance limits of minimum 2 and maximum 30.
opzione_b: Enable automatic scaling on ASP-Prod, set Maximum burst to 30, and set Always ready instances to 2 for each app.
opzione_c: An autoscale setting that contains a recurrence profile scheduled for Fridays from 18:00 to 23:00 with higher instance limits, in addition to the default profile that has lower instance limits.
opzione_d: Scale up ASP-Prod to the Isolated v2 tier and manually set the instance count to 20.
spiegazione: Option c is correct. Microsoft Learn documents the recurrence profile as the autoscale profile type used for a day or set of days of the week, and states that autoscale evaluates profiles in the order fixed-date, recurring, then default, using the first suitable profile found. A recurrence profile for Fridays 18:00-23:00 with raised instance limits therefore takes effect on schedule and provisions capacity before the predictable spike arrives, while the default profile keeps limits - and cost - low the rest of the time. Autoscale supports up to 20 profiles per setting, and it is available on Standard and up, so a Premium v3 plan qualifies. Option a is wrong because a single metric-based default profile is purely reactive: instances are only added after CPU has already risen for the rule's duration, which conflicts with the requirement to have capacity in place when the event starts and with the requirement not to rely on metric thresholds alone. Option b is wrong because automatic scaling is traffic-based only - Learn explicitly states it has no schedule-based scaling and advises using autoscale instead if you need time-based scaling. It is also reactive, so it does not pre-provision for a known event window. Option d is wrong because it is manual and permanent: 20 Isolated v2 instances would run continuously regardless of load, which is the opposite of minimizing cost, and it requires an App Service Environment plus a separately charged virtual network.
tags: app service, autoscale, recurrence profile, scheduled scaling, premium v3, cost optimization, azure monitor
